translation: Perhaps because Miho and Satsuki often meet locally, they have identical expressions and ways of speaking.
Their way of eating sweets was particularly similar; both were carrying small pieces of cookie to their mouths with their manicured hands.
I wonder if it has always been like this, but when I try to remember, my memory is vague.
I wonder if the small quirks and gestures they had when we met before have already drifted somewhere else.
Miho is now married, bought a used detached house in her hometown, and often has friends gather there.

Even though I sometimes feel reluctant about part-time work tomorrow too, being the only point of contact with the world outside of convenience stores and a valuable opportunity to interact with "ordinary women in their thirties" of the same age, I try to respond as much as possible to Miho's invitation.
Today, Miho, Yukari with her still small child, Satsuki who is married but has no kids yet, and I were at Miho's house having tea and sharing a cake.
It was then, for the first time, I felt I could become a part of the world.
I felt as though I had just been born.
On this day, I was certainly born as a normal part of the world.
For two weeks leading up to the opening, we formed pairs, practiced relentlessly facing imaginary customers, and dealt with employees.
Smiling and bowing to the customer, putting sanitary products in a paper bag, separating hot items from cold ones, and sanitizing hands with alcohol when asked for fast food.

The cash register contained real money to get used to it, but the receipt was marked with "Training" in big letters, and the other party were part-time colleagues dressed in the same uniform, so it felt like we were playing a pretend shopping game.
My younger sister, two years my junior, was unlike me a "normal" child.
Yet she didn't avoid me, on the contrary, she rather admired me.
When my younger sister was scolded by our mother for some ordinary matter, differing from me, I approached our mother and asked, "Why are you angry?"
Every time my lecture ended because I interrogated my mother, my sister, thinking she was protected, always said "Thank you" to me.
Since I wasn't very interested in toys and sweets, I often gave them to my younger sister.
Therefore, my younger sister was always following me around.
"Dad likes grilled chicken, so let's cook and eat this today," I say clearly again in case he didn't hear me the first time.
My mother looks surprised, and another child's mother nearby also seems shocked, her eyes, nostrils and mouth all opening wide simultaneously.
His face was so strange that I felt like laughing, but seeing him gaze at my hands, I thought to myself, one is not enough.
"Should I get more?"
As she glanced at some sparrows walking in a row nearby, my mother, who finally came to her senses, desperately shouted in a reproachful voice, "Keiko!"
"Let's make a grave for the little bird and bury it.
Look, everyone is crying too.
It's sad when a friend dies, isn't it?
"Poor thing, isn't it?"
"Why? Despite finally being dead," my question left my mother speechless.
He quickly put canned coffee, cigarettes, and an American hot dog into a small bag.
In the meantime, the man who had been jingling the small change in his pocket suddenly seemed to have a thought and slipped his hand into his breast pocket.
From that gesture, I instantly deduced that he was going to pay with electronic money.
"Welcome, good morning!"
She gives a slight bow and accepts the can of coffee offered by the male customer.
"Ah, also one of the number 5 cigarettes.
"Understood.
Quickly pulling out a Marlboro Light Menthol and scanning it at the register.
"Please touch for age verification.
While touching the screen, he saw the man's gaze shift smoothly to the showcase full of fast food, and he stopped his fingers.
"I could ask 'Would you like anything else? but if the customer seems to be hesitating about making a purchase, I prefer to take a step back and wait.
Reacting to the faint clinking of change, I turned around and looked towards the cash register.
Many people who jingle coins in their hands or pockets tend to buy cigarettes or newspapers quickly and go back, so they are sensitive to the sound of money.
Sure enough, there was a man approaching the register with a can of coffee in one hand and his other hand stuck in his pocket.
I quickly moved around the store and slipped behind the cash register, standing ready so as not to keep the customers waiting.
The convenience store is filled with sound.
The sound of a chime as customers enter, over the store's speakers an idol advertises new products.
The sound of barcodes being scanned, amidst the shop assistant's call.
The sound of items being put into a basket, the crinkling of bread bags, and the clicking of heels walking around the store.
Everything is mixed together, becoming the "sound of the convenience store", constantly touching my eardrums.
